Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 42, to amend the criminal code (Trustees defined. Disposition of fines).
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The bill is rather a simple one. The first section provides for an amendment to the interpretation clause in regard to the word "trustee." "Trustee" in the criminal code is defined as a trustee appointed under deed, will or other instrument in writing. The amendment is to include trustees who will be named under an act of parliament.
The other amendment is in regard to the application of fines. Generally speaking, all fines imposed, save those in regard to revenue, go to the treasurers of the various provinces to be disposed of as they see fit. There is in the present section a special clause in regard to Ontario allowing certain fines to go to the municipalities. The idea is to put Ontario on the same basis as the other provinces in respect to these fines. The matter was litigated recently and a case went to the judicial committee last autumn in regard to a large fine which was imposed in Toronto some years ago.

The house resumed from Monday, April 4, consideration in committee of Bill No. 20, to amend the Petroleum and Naphtha Inspection Act-Mr. Ryckman-Mr. Tummon in the chair.
On section 1-Tests of petroleum.

Mr. Chairman, when this bill was last before the committee I was troubled by some matters which appear to be cleared up in the general statute, chapter 159 of the revised statutes of Canada. First, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to clause 2 of the act, the interpretation clause, subsection (j), where specific gravity is defined. As mentioned by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), it is quite true that these tests were taken at about 60 degrees. From section (j) I read the following:
"Specific gravity" means the weight of any fluid as compared with the weight of distilled water, both being at the temperature of 62 degrees by Fahrenheit's thermometer, the barometer standing at thirty inches; and specific gravity is expressed by stating in pounds and hundredths of a pound the weight of a gallon of the fluid compared or to be compared.
There is a schedule attached to the act, which defines the mode of testing, and specifies
the pyrometer. Following the specifications for the pyrometer or testing apparatus are directions for applying the flash test. These directions are very minute, and they show how important it is that the temperature should be given every attention. For instance, if the room be too cold the temperature must be brought up; if it be too warm it has to be lowered. The amendment proposes only that there shall be a change in subsection (b) of section 10. There are three subsections in section 10, and all must be complied with. If I may be permitted I shall read the three clauses in section 10. They are as follows:
(a)	If, when tested by the pyrometer
described in the schedule to this act, at a lower temperature than eighty-five degrees by Fahrenheit's thermometer, it emits a vapour that will flash; or,	_
(b)	if it weighs more than eight pounds and seventeen hundredths of a pound per gallon; or,
(c)	if it weighs less than seven pounds and seventy-five hundredths of a pound per gallon.
As we are aware the suggestion is that the seventeen-hundredths of specific gravity should be changed to four-tenths. Section 10 has been in the statutes for a long time; I know it was in the revised statutes of 1886. As has been certified this change can have no deleterious effect, and the effect may be beneficial. The temperatures are settled by the act through the clauses I have given.
While this matter is of a somewhat technical nature I hope hon. members will feel they understand the proposal, that it is only a minor change in the specific gravity arrived at by the test prescribed in the act itself in accordance with the schedule.

Section agreed to.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 4, to amend the Patent Act (as amended).
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Tummon in the chair.
On section	1-Conflicting applications:
notice to applicants.

Mr. Chairman, I may say that since this 'bill passed its second reading it has been considered by a special committee of this house. I do not think any committee could be more patient than that committee has been in hearing the representations made by those interested in patents, and especially by the representative patent lawyers of the country. The bill is reported with amendments, and the entire committee concurred in the amendments suggested.
The first section of this bill deals with conflicting applications for patents. Formerly such patents were referred to arbitration under section 22 of the Patent Act. In 1923 parliament passed an amendment to the effect that, after arbitration proceedings were initiated, either party to those proceedings might apply to the exchequer court for the determination of the conflict, and that thereupon no further proceedings should be taken by arbitration. The result has been that in order to obtain access to the exchequer court arbitration proceedings have necessarily been begun, which were very expensive to the prospective litigants, and then, after considerable expenditure had been made by the one or both parties in preparation for the arbitration, on the application of one of the contestants, the whole case came within the jurisdiction of the exchequer court. After thoroughly considering the matter and in the hope of avoiding these circumlocutory proceedings and obviating expense for applicants for patents who could ill afford to bear that expense, the committee has unanimously adopted the proposed amendments to section 22. Some changes were made, ibut section 22,

as now expressed in section 1 of this bill, has received the unanimous approval of the committee, and I think I may say the unanimous approval of all the experts who appeared before the committee. I therefore move that section 1 be adopted.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Invalid claims not to affect valid claims.

This section is important in this respect. It has been held by our courts that in an action for the infringement of a patent, if there were one valid claim in the application and several which were invalid, effect would be given to the valid claim. But the contrary is true if the action is one in which a patent is sought to be impeached. The committee concurred unanimously in this section, which abolishes any distinction between the two kinds of action. The section now provides that in any action or proceeding respecting a patent, whether it be an action for impeachment or for infringement, which contains two or more claims, when one or more of such claims are held to be valid, but another or others invalid and void, effect shall be given to the patent as if it contained only the valid claim or claims, so that all of the issues in the controversy before the court may be decided by the court.
I move adoption of the section.

Section agreed to.
Sections 3 to 5 inclusive agreed to.

Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 27, to amend the Excise Act.

This section deals with the administration of the act and is important from the viewpoint of the department. However, I do not think there can be any difference of opinion as to the working out of the provisions. This section defines a provincial analyst as follows:
"Provincial analyst" means any analyst appointed by the government of any province and having authority to make any analysis for any public purpose.

certain points throughout the dominion there are analysts, who have not been appointed directly by the provincial governments but who have received authority to make tests and analyses. This section will permit the services of these analysts to be used in an official capacity.

This section will permit
the minister to give to the commissioner of excise the power to sign revocation of licences to brew beer. At the present time this takes up considerable time of the minister. None of the functions
covered by the section to be amended are important?

The authority granted by
this section is analogous to that given to the commissioner of customs in connection with seizures.

I may say so, in a lesser degree. Where conviction has been made for an infraction of the liquor laws of the provinces, it has been our practice to cancel any licence held by the offender.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Recovery of penalties.

This is a matter of
administration and I can best explain it by reading the note. It is as follows:
The section as it stands provides for trial of excise offences before a judge of a county court, or before a police or stipendiary magistrate or any two justices of the peace. There are other functionaries vested by the provincial legislatures with the powers of two justices of the peace, e.g., the chief magistrates of Prince Edward Island, but who do not come within any of the classes specifically described above. Doubt has arisen as to whether such persons have jurisdiction to try offences under the Excise Act, and it is thought expedient to confer such jurisdiction upon them specifically.
This is merely an effort to arrive at uniformity of administration.

Section agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are nearing the fifteenth of the month when in the ordinary course certain expenditures will have to be made, and if the house is agreeable I should like to ask for interim supply. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are asking for onesixth with the exception of certain special items, where we are asking for one-quarter. This is necessary if we are to function smoothly in the matter of the payment of our accounts. The new system of accounting requires that money must be voted and available in order to be ear-marked before commitments are made. The special votes in connection with which we are asking for one-quarter are Nos. 35 and 36, covering the Senate and the House of Commons. When the Senate and House of Commons are in session we are at the peak of our expenditure in connection with these votes. With respect to vote 45, experimental farms, we are asking one-fourth for that as well, because this being seeding time, it is the time of year when the largest experiments in the department are made. We are asking the same with respect to vote 186, geological survey, mines. At this period of the year the parties are leaving for the field and they must be placed in funds. Many of them live in remote areas not near to banks, and they must take actual money with them. Under our new system of accounting where there is no opportunity of switching accounts or of utilizing other funds, as was the case in the old days, when perhaps one-twelfth might suffice, the vote must be available in full. Another item is 207, care of patients under the Department of Pensions. This vote is very heavily called upon at the present time. It is an item which is largely uncontrollable and doctors' bills are flowing in from all parts of the country. The overhead at this time is therefore particularly heavy. Item 209 is for pensions. This is for pay and

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the committee, but it seems that the matter of pensions is one to which 41761-113
this house and country,must pay attention. I received information from the Board of Pension Commissioners the other day, and from it I learned that at that point there are 23,900 applicants for pensions, that in the pension tribunals there are 2,650, and before the appeal court there are 1,316, making a total of nearly
30,000	applicants for pensions to-day. I think it is quite apparent to everyone in this house that at the rate those cases are being heard they will never be disposed of in the history of man. Those applicants are dying all over the country, and they have not yet been given an opportunity to be heard. Parliament in its wisdom, or its unwisdom, gave these boys the right to be heard. That right having been granted, neither parliament nor the country is justified in putting any impediment in the way of its being exercised. It is quite apparent that with thirty thousand cases before the tribunals now the machinery is absolutely inadequate to function successfully.
I am going to make a suggestion to the minister-I have made it to the Prime Minister a good many times in the last few years -that we conscript the county judges to hear the cases in the first instance. I see the difficulty of creating more machinery, and I do not think we should do so, because in a year or two we would have a large number of officials on our hands with nothing to do, and the difficulty would be to get rid of them. More than that, we would have difficulty in getting the proper class of men to act. Consequently if we conscript the county judges to hear the cases in the first instance, those cases could be cleared off in about twelve months. Then I would convert the Board of Pension Commissioners into an executive body. Finally I would throw the tribunals and the appeal court together and make the combined body a court of appeal. I do not see why one man should not constitute a court of appeal. Then we could have enough courts to handle the appeals in ten or twelve months and give these men an opportunity to exercise the right that parliament said they should have. I feel we are not doing justice to the men, and we are not doing justice to ourselves, for having granted them the right to be heard, we are not justified in putting any impediments in the way of their exercising that right. I make this suggestion to the minister because I am so thoroughly co'n-vinced that otherwise these thirty thousand cases cannot be successfully handled.

Mr. Chairman, in common with the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) and other hon. members who have been for some years members of the pension committee, I have been greatly concerned with the present situation of thousands of applicants awaiting decisions on their cases. I am of the opinion that we have about all the legislation we need; I think the act as it stands is a good act and that it fairly well covers the necessities of the occasion, but we run into difficulties when we consider the machinery for carrying out the intentions of the act. I think it may be taken for granted that the people of Canada as a whole, that every hon. member of this house and any government which may be in power is anxious that these men should be dealt with properly. There is complete unanimity in that respect but the people of Canada as well as hon. members of this house have been wondering for a long time why it is that their intentions

Supply-Pensions
179a
so definitely expressed have not been put into force. In speaking in this way we are not trying to be critical of the minister or of the government, we are simply suggesting that perhaps it may be necessary to go a little further in simplifying and amplifying the machinery of the act. Perhaps in an attempt to be solicitous for those who are deserving of pension and to see that no one not deserving shall slip in, we have made the machinery too cumbersome for its purpose. As stated by the hon. member for Muskoka, there are in the neighbourhood of 30,000 applicants awaiting consideration, many of whom have been waiting since the time the act came into force in 1930.
And some before that.

Yes, and some before that, although I am speaking of the applications made under the new act. That is a long time for men to wait who are rapidly sinking into premature old age or who are hopelessly ill.
I have discussed the suggestions made by the hon. member for Muskoka with the hon. member himself and with others. I am not quite certain that his suggestions are the best, but I have not heard any others which offer any improvement. After all, there is a body of men scattered throughout the country who, on the whole, hold the respect of the people for their knowledge of law, their ability to sift evidence and their honesty and fairness of purpose. Whatever we may say about the salaries paid, we all agree that our judiciary is a body of men which can be depended upon to give fair opinions and decisions. Although they are not trained in this particular act, which is very intricate, they are properly trained in the sifting of evidence and even though the most of the evidence offered in these cases is of a medical character, the judiciary has had certain experience in the consideration of this type of testimony in the trial of civil damage and other suits.
It is obvious to all of us, and particularly to those who have been working on pension matters from year to year, that hundreds of these men are losing not only hope for the future but confidence in the country for which they fought and which promised to look after them. They are losing confidence in the legislation :by which this country has endeavoured to carry out its promises. When the committee met a couple of years ago and evolved the present machinery it was thought it would be fairly ample for every contingency, that the cases would be handled with reasonable expedition and that there would be very 41761-1135
little accumulation by this time. It is obvious that the committee was mistaken and that the machinery, effective though it may be within its limits, is not able to cope with the tremendous accumulation of applications which has occurred. Humanity dictates that we must supplement the present machinery with something else which will prove effective 'but, as the hon. member for Muskoka has said, we must not set up a tremendous machine to employ hundreds of men which after the accumulation has been taken care of will constitute a problem with which this country will have to deal. The suggestions offered may not be the best, but I would impress upon the minister and the government the need of immediate attention to this matter. If no other suggestions are put forward, it is due to this house and to the men chiefly interested that the suggestions which have been offered should be weighed and considered in a careful and sympathetic manner.
The minister may remember that twelve months ago I spoke in this chamber in connection with a particular case, that of a man by the name of Martin. The minister was good enough to interest himself in this case which was expedited so far as a hearing by a tribunal was concerned. This man had his hearing months and months ago but, as is the case with nearly every favourable decision, his case was referred to the appeal court where apparently it has been buried. In the meantime, the man is sinking rapidly. Such action is not fair to the man and it is objected to by all his friends. These people know his condition; they attended the hearing at the tribunal and having heard the decision, took it for granted that the man had won his case. The delay in a final decision 'has created a very bad feeling among all those with whom he was acquainted. This man's case is typical of hundreds and thousands of other cases.
I say now, as I have said before, that I am not in favour of the present provision which permits an appeal on the part of the commission from a favourable decision by a tribunal. The men who meet the applicant face to face are able to size him up, and I have always held that they are best able to decide, from their personal impression of the man, whether or not his case is a just one. I have felt that the final authority should lie somewhere, and I have regarded the tribunal as the logical body in whom it should lie. The law provides otherwise, however, and to some degree it has resulted in protecting the treasury. But to a greater degree it has increased the delay and the cumbersome nature of the machinery. I would suggest, therefore,
Supply-Pensions

that when the proposal of the hon. member for Muskoka is weighed, those judges, if they are appointed, or whoever is appointed to look after the matter, should be given some power of finality, so that when they have heard a case it will not be merely the disposition of one stage of the proceedings, simply piling up in greater numbers cases that must be finally disposed of subsequently. If appeal from their judgment is necessary something might be done along the line suggested by the hon. member, which was in effect this: that the present members of the pension tribunals might be utilized as judges of appeal, divided into several courts of perhaps three members in each. These experienced men who are now engaged in the work might then form a sort of enlarged appeal court by means of which the whole matter might be expedited. Every man in this chamber and in the country as well has in mind the absolute necessity of dealing with this question and dealing with it in time to be of some good to the men for whose benefit the act was passed. I am not speaking critically; the mistake was mine as well as every other member's, because I took part in the committee in setting up this machinery, and my hopes have been frustrated, as have the hopes of every other member of that committee. It is obvious that it is not the fault of the minister or of the government itself. The fact is that the machinery we set up, under the conditions in which we set it up, was inadequate to meet the situation. But the situation must be dealt with, and lacking a better suggestion-and I for one am prepared to accept any suggestion from any quarter which might meet the situation-I would urge that this proposal that has been made be not turned down without the most careful and sympathetic consideration.

I rise to make a plea on
behalf of the returned soldiers who are applying for pension in the smaller centres. I had not the privilege of hearing the address of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mc-Gibbon), but I gather from the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man), that he suggested something about county judges having jurisdiction over the matter. I had hoped to discuss that very subject when we were last considering this question. Like the hon. member for Red Deer, I have no fault to find with the legislation; but I do find fault, as the returned men themselves find fault, with the machinery which has been set up under that legislation. That machinery is too cumbersome. We did not realize exactly the extent to which appli-[Mr. Speakman.l
cations for pensions would be made, and now we find that in the smaller centres the men are not having their cases heard by the pension tribunal. The minister the other night intimated that the members of the tribunal are working at full capacity, and I have no doubt that he is correct; but may I cite one specific example which I am sure is typical throughout Canada. In the county of Lambton, in the city of Sarnia, no tribunal has met although for over a j'ear, as I am informed by the Canadian Legion, some twenty-eight or thirty cases have been waiting to be disposed of. It is true the tribunal have met in London, but all the cases they can handle there are those from the county of Middlesex and the city of London, and it is recognized pretty general^ that they are unable to sit in the various county towns throughout the provinces. For this reason returned soldiers throughout the dominion find that their cases cannot be heard, while, as pointed out by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs), men are dying and going to their graves without the relief that was promised by their country and in the legislation itself when it was adopted.
I submit that in order to speed, up the matter some additional machinery should be created. To this end .1 was going to suggest the appointment of the county judges. With all respect to them, I submit that in the majority of counties, especially in the smaller county towns, the county judges are not overworked, and I am sure that they would undertake the work without extra pay. This would obviate any additional expense to the government, and the judges would be able to administer the act just as well as any tribunal; for after all it is only the administration of a statute. As the hon. member for Red Deer has pointed out, the judges are used to hearing evidence and they would know the various . applicants who would come before them. Everything considered, we should be able to clear the decks and have justice done the soldiers. In addition to that, may I point out to the minister that it would be, in the end, a real economy to the country. It may be said that there are some centres where the countjr judges are overworked and therefore would be unable to deal with the situation. In such centres an additional county judge might be appointed for the duration of the act. I suggest, therefore, that the members of the tribunal be left to sit on cases as they are now doing in such centres as Toronto, Windsor and the larger places, but that in the smaller centres-in the county I have the honour to represent and in the

Supply-Pensions
large majority of other counties-some action be taken to expedite the proceedings and to see that the returned soldiers shall get a square deal through the administration of the act.
I am not complaining of the act, nor am I finding any fault with the minister; what I am complaining of is the machinery under which the act is administered. May I suggest also that in the smaller centres the pensions advocates are not giving, in the preparation of cases, that assistance which they should. To some extent this is no doubt the fault of the men themselves; but it has been my experience, and no doubt the experience of other members of the house, that the great bulk of the work has fallen upon the shoulders of the Canadian legion, who are doing it gratuitously in their spare time. They are working without any remuneration but merely in the hope that their reward will be the granting of pensions to those men whom they are helping. In the majority of cases, members of the legion or, where this is not so, others who are patriotic enough to assist in the preparation of cases, are doing the work. I do not think that is fair, and rather than pay large salaries to advocates I would suggest that in those centres some allowance might be made to the men of the legion and others of that sort who are giving valuable assistance.
I do urge the minister to see that the work of hearing applicants be speeded up. I am sure that anything that may be done to bring this about will meet with the unanimous approval of all parties in the house, and I urge upon the minister and the government to consider it. I gather from the remarks he has made in reply to the hon. member for North Battleford and others that it has not been definitely decided by the government not to introduce legislation this session. Let us have it in ample time, and if it is intended merely to establish additional machinery I am sure that we on this side of the house will support it.

It would appear to me that as regards the northern part of Saskatchewan, at least the part I represent in the Commons, two main difficulties confront the returned men. One is in regard to those who are on the land and I intend to say something about that later on when that item comes up. The other is in regard to the pension question that we are now discussing. I asked the minister, I think twice this session, whether the government was considering the matter of bringing down new legislation in connection with returned men, and I think
the hon. member for Red Deer also asked the question once, but so far the minister. has given the answer simply that the matter is under consideration. In other words, no definite answer is given and we do not know in the Commons, and I am satisfied that the returned men throughout Canada have no idea as yet whether anything is to be done this session or not. My conclusion, from the answer of the minister, has been that we are not going to have any new legislation this session. If I am correct in that assumption, I think the returned men throughout Canada ought to know about it. The government ought to have its mind made up by this time whether it is going to do anything in the way of ameliorative legislation this session or not, and if not, the quicker that fact is known, the better; there is no use in delaying it.
Apart from that there is the question of the act. I think the act is all right or about all right. The administration of it is the difficulty. Some think we have too much machinery; some think we have not enough, and others think we ought to add to it. Thousands of cases are waiting to be settled; progress is not taking place as it should and the returned men are becoming very much dissatisfied. I was wondering whether the minister could not have a conference with the pension board, the tribunal and other bodies to discuss the whole situation in an endeavour to arrive at some conclusion whether the suggestions made here to-day can be acted upon, whether anything can be done to improve the administration of the act, and thus hasten the hearing of those thousands of cases that are at present clogging the administrative machinery.
I appreciate the answers the minister has given me so far.	I know he occupies a difficult position.	I know the
problem requires thought	and perhaps
the government's mind has not as yet been made up, but I believe in the interests of the returned men throughout Canada they ought to know whether they are to expect anything in the way of legislation this session. They ought to know this at once. It is very important that anything that can be done to hasten the hearing of all these cases should be done, because I know in the North Battle-ford riding we have many cases that have not yet been heard, and the returned men there are not very well pleased. They are working hand in hand with the legion and all the other soldier organizations to get action. I have done my best to cooperate with them apart from politics at all, yet many cases have not been settled and as has been mentioned here this afternoon, if they are not settled soon
Supply-Pensions

the men will pass away and redress will be impossible. I would therefore be glad if the minister, while we are in committee on this question, could deal with one or two of those phases in such a way as to send out at least a note of encouragement to the men throughout Canada who are expecting redress and who so far have not received it.

I desire to mention just two difficulities with which I have met in connection with this legislation. I well realize that the committee who drafted this legislation hoped it would meet the situation. It was hoped that the judges who actually saw the applicant for pension and who heard the evidence which he and his witnesses gave, would be the final judges as to whether he should receive a pension or not. Great disappointment has been created in many instances where, after a case has been worked out and a favourable decision obtained from the tribunal, it has been found that the government advocate has appealed the case and then, after long months of waiting, that the appeal board has turned it down on some technicality. I know there are many cases before the appeal board, 'but this has been a very disappointing feature in connection with the working out of the legislation.
There is also the old difficulty of diagnosis. If a certain diagnosis is chosen, it might be worked on for months or years and finally there might be disagreement in regard to it. It seems too bad there is not some judge who could give a man a pension either on the diagnosis chosen or for whatever his trouble is or whatever the judge thinks it is. It is unfair that these men should be denied the privilege of pension through no fault of their pwn, but simply because of a difference of opinion as regards diagnosis.

I should like to say
a word in support of the general idea of some effort being made to speed up the work of determining whether men are entitled to pension or not. From my observation it would seem to me that if the present plan is followed, many of these men will go to their graves before we or the country will know whether they are pensionable cases. In the portion of northern Ontario in which I live, I know of cases where I have been making every effort I could, where the Great War Veterans have been doing the same thing and where the Canadian Legion are constantly trying to bring cases to trial, so to speak, but where men have been waiting for two years or more, ever since the last legislation was passed, and do not seem to be

any nearer getting before a tribunal than when they started.
The statement made yesterday about tribunals going into certain districts and spending a day hearing certain cases and then going on to another district, is true so far as northern Ontario is concerned. I know of men who have been notified that a tribunal would be in a certain place on a certain day and who have travelled a hundred miles to be there that day, only to find, just before their cases were to come up, that the tribunal had moved on to another place. I believe if the proposal of the hon. member for Mus-lcoka-Ontario, which was supported by my hon. friends opposite, whereby district court judges could be conscripted for this work, were adopted, it would facilitate at least the primary part of the work and send the men on, if necessary, to a court of appeal. These judges are men trained in taking and weighing evidence; the applicant comes before them for a pension; the medical officers are there and they are in a position to decide, I think as carefully and accurately as any group of men who could be found anywhere. Surely the country has an obligation to say to those soldiers:	You are or you are not entitled
to receive a pension. The fact that we are now fourteen years from the conclusion of the war and that there are still some 26,000 or 27,000 applicants for pensions whose cases have not been heard and who have no idea when they will be, does not speak well for the administration of the act. Whether the county judges are the right ones or not will, I presume, be for parliament to decide, but certainly some steps should be taken to bring this matter to a conclusion and let the country and the returned men know who are entitled to pension and who are not. The cases are becoming so long drawn out and the dissatisfaction which is being created is such that one can hardly express the feelings these returned men have for what seems to them to be a deliberate neglect of what they look upon as an inherent right to have their cases thoroughly examined and a final decision made.

I should like to make a few observations relative to the working out of the present pension legislation. First I should like to make it very clear that so far as I have been able to ascertain there is no disposition on the part of the ex-service men to blame anybody in particular because of the present delay. The facts are, as hon. members of the house who were then present, are well aware, that in 1930 the whole matter of pension legislation was reviewed by a

Supply-Pensions
committee of this house. That committee in conjunction with representatives of the exservice men worked out amendments to the then existing legislation with a view to solving the question. That the legislation has not worked out as well as anticipated is not a matter for blame of the government or of the ex-service men or of the members of the committee. I think it is conceded by all that the pension legislation passed in 1930 and as amended in 1931 had in view facilitating the hearing of claims for pensions and their adjudication, but in the working out of that legislation certain defects have become obvious. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister not in any critical mood but as the result of considerable inquiry from the men who are involved and from the officers of the various organizations representing the men.
As far as I have been able to ascertain, the present congestion occurs at two points; first, before the Board of Pension Commissioners. I believe that to-day there are before that board approximately 23,000 cases. The number was greatly increased by reason of the amendment introduced in 1931, which had the effect of referring back to the Board of Pension Commissioners all those cases which had previously been refused by them. The reason for the referring back was because of that provision which is ordinarily known as the benefit-of-the-doubt clause, which was introduced in 1931. I am not going into that in detail because it is familiar to all who have studied the question. But as the result of that 1931 amendment there was referred back to the board cases which they had previously dealt with to the number of 15,311. Since the passing of the 1931 amendment more than 14,000 cases have been dealt with by the Board of Pension Commissioners, but there stand unadjudicated to-day more than
23,000	cases. At the present rate it is estimated that it will take years and years to adjudicate upon the cases already before them. Pension applicants making application to-day find that even with the machinery operating at maximum speed it will be years before their case can be determined.
As to the steps that should be taken to alleviate the congestion at the initial point, I am not going to elaborate. I understand that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has made certain suggestions. I feel that the minister and the department are fully seized of the situation, and to put it in a plain, frank way, I think it is up to the department to work out some method, whether it is the method suggested or not, whereby the
hearings before the Board of Pension Commissioners can be speeded up, and speeded up very considerably.
So far as the tribunals or the secondary courts are concerned, my opinion is that they are getting on very well indeed and that at the present time they are not in any sense congested. They are able at the present time to take care very comfortably of the cases that come before them, but in view of the fact that so many of the cases heard by the tribunals and decided in favour of the applicants are appealed on instructions from the Board of Pension Commissioners, we find congestion again before the appeal court, and there is the place where the present congestion is most marked. I have in mind a particular instance. Individual cases prove nothing perhaps, but this is a case which has been pending since 1927 to which I wish to draw attention. A favourable decision was granted in 1930. The case was referred to the court of appeal. I have investigated the record and I find that the applicant was dealt with very generously by the court of appeal. They found upon going into the facts that in their opinion a favourable award was not justified and they referred the case back to the tribunal, suggesting that further evidence was necessary on certain points and giving the applicant the opportunity to adduce further evidence. That case went back, was heard, and a second decision was given in favour of the applicant. The case was appealed again, on instructions from the Board of Pension Commissioners- I am not saying whether they were right or wrong in doing it-and now it is held up again by the court of appeal. I have visited that court and have looked up their records. There is congestion. But it is not their fault. I think they are doing as much as is humanly possible, but it is not possible for them to hear and determine expeditiously all the cases that are coming before them.
Ex-service men and their organizations, rightly or wrongly, feel that too great a percentage of the cases determined favourably to applicants by the tribunals are being appealed, and therefore delayed. The psychological effect throughout this country is very, very bad. Take the case I instanced. It is the case of a widow. She is at present ill and penniless, living on charity in a third-rate hotel in the city of Winnipeg. There have been two decisions in her favour and yet the matter comes before the court of appeal again and is there awaiting decision.
Mere criticism is of no value in itself unless some suggestion can be made. I draw to the attention of the minister-I know that he has
Supply-Pensions

perused it-and to the attention of the house the joint considered opinion of the various ex-service men's associations, presented to the government with certain suggestions. Briefly, their suggestions relative to relieving the congestion in the appeal court are, first, that more care should be exercised by the Board of Pension Commissioners before they order an appeal from a favourable decision by the tribunal. Secondly, that inasmuch as the court of appeal consists of only three members, and the tribunal of twelve, sitting in threes, and in view of the large percentage of appeals coming up from the tribunals to the court of appeal, that court has more to do than it can handle. The suggestion has been made by joint committees of all the organizations that the court of appeal be enlarged-but in such a way as to involve no additional expense in administration-by making available for decisions in review the full membership of the tribunals. Roughly, the suggestion is that the same chairman of the court of appeal be retained, and that the legislation be amended so that the court of appeal may call upon any two members of the tribunal to sit in with the chairman and review cases. If that system were adopted, instead of one court of appeal consisting of three men there could be about fifteen men sitting, and five courts could be in operation instead of one.
' By that method there would be no additions to the personnel of the present machinery, no increase in the expense of administration, and there would be the advantage of expediting the hearing of appeals. Further, there would be coordination of the work of the appeal court and the trial courts.
Rightly or wrongly the feeling is abroad that there is not proper coordination between the court of appeal and the tribunals, the trial courts. The witnesses come before the trial courts sitting at given centres. Those courts hear the witnesses, observe their demeanour and weigh the evidence. It is a well known principle of law that an appellate court will not reverse the decision of a trial court upon matters of fact-on matters of law, yes, but on matters of fact, no, unless it is obvious there has been a gross miscarriage of justice. In view of the fact that 60 per cent or more of the cases decided before the tribunals in favour of the applicants are appealed, and approximately 75 per cent of the appeals are allowed, there is a feeling that something is wrong, and that through lack of coordination between the two courts a weakness exists. There is a belief that if members of the trial courts were allowed to sit in on the appellate courts they would gain

experience both in the trial and appellate divisions, and as a result there would be better administration of justice and greater expedition in the administration of the act.
There are two points for consideration. First, there is the congestion which cannot for years and years be relieved with the present machinery. Secondly, we know of cases which have been heard before the appellate court wherein the applicants have received favourable decisions, and yet because of appeals being filed in the meantime they could get no relief. We know of cases where applicants have received favourable decisions from trial courts. Those decisions have been appealed and the applicants have had to wait six months or a year for the hearing of their cases. In the .meantime they may be in want, in destitute circumstances, and urgently in need of medical attention which they do not receive. I may receive the answer, "Oh well, ultimately the appeal court will decide in their favour, and the decisions would be retroactive." The answer is that many of them die in the meantime, and many others suffer hardships. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, although I know the minister is endeavouring to do everything within his power, and that these matters are constantly in his mind, I earnestly urge upon him to consider, not at another session but before this session closes, the making of certain amendments to the existing legislation which will expedite the hearing of cases.

I think the hon. member who has just taken his seat has laid his finger upon most of the sores in connection with thi3 matter. Probably I would do well to review the progress which has been made at various times in an endeavour to satisfy the returned men. I think all people are convinced, when they look at the large sums of money which have been spent in an endeavour to give the returned men satisfaction for the sacrifices they made, that there has been no great effort to economize.
The procedure we have known for years and years arose from the formation of the Board of Pension Commissioners. That body had absolute control in the matter of the pensions of ex-service men. All men who have served know about the activities of the pensions board. As time went on there was a feeling, first that the actions of that body were arbitrary; secondly, that cases were heard in camera, and that the men who gave decisions concerning the eligibility of applicants to pensions did not see the applicants. Because of that condition the board of appeal

was formed, and the two organizations I have named worked for some years. But as the hon. member who has just spoken has said, there was no coordination or cooperation between or standardization in those two bodies. There was a feeling that jealousy existed between them, that they were working contrary to and criticizing each other.
Then we came to the committee of 1930. When the statement is made that ex-service men are dissatisfied, the reply might be made: "Well, this is your own legislation." I should like to say, however, that in the committee of 1930 every attempt was made to keep free from partisanship. The legislation under which we are now operating is the result of an endeavour by the returned men to wipe' out difficulties and get away from dissatisfaction. Consequently, arising out of a decision of a meeting of returned men in Regina, the suggestion was made that tribunals be formed, and that they be empowered to sit on cases after they had been heard by the Board of Pension Commissioners. Then, the court of appeal formed the third court. So that no matter what government was in power, and no matter who may have been the minister, undoubtedly there was the greatest endeavour to give satisfaction.
Here is where the difficulty arose: Throughout the meetings of that committee we were constantly informed that the Board of Pension Commissioners were overburdened, and were unable to deal adequately with the applications. But what happened? The legislation not only placed upon the Board of Pension Commissioners all the burden they already had, but sent back to them all the cases that had been commuted and all the cases that had been dismissed. It was pointed out in committee then:	If the Board of Pension
Commissioners are overburdened at the present time, how in the world are they going to function when this additional burden is thrown upon them? It was my belief at that time-and I did not support the legislation; the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) stood with me-that this was bound to fail. In short, you were going to plug the machinery right at the beginning. And it has turned out just as we predicted. I am afraid we are again in this position, that we are not getting cooperation between the Board of Pension Commissioners and the tribunals. It may be that one is too hard and the other is too easy, but there is no cooperation. You have two courts reviewing cases. The Board of Pension Commissioners review each application. They do not say, "We dismiss the application." They just simply say
in their letter, "We do not grant this." Then they add, "You may take this now to the chief advocate of the tribunal." If there was some cooperation and the reason was given why the application was refused, it would save a whole lot of reviewing and would give the tribunals a better opportunity to go on with their work. But imagine the position. Here is legislation directing that the case be reviewed thoroughly by the Board of Pension Commissioners. They do not grant the application, therefore the case goes to the tribunal. It is taken to the tribunal by the advocate. Someone says the advocates do not work. I differ absolutely with that statement; they do work. But the advocate has got to go through the mill with the case, and when he is satisfied it is ready for hearing it is brought up. A little bit of standardization of opinion would save all the delay. Suppose it was announced: "We have sat on this case in camera; now we will throw it open and submit it to the tribunal." I do not think "tribunal" is the appropriate title. In my opinion the apt title would be "travelling pension board." If this travelling pension board were part of the Board of Pension Commissioners, the men would not be disposed to appeal their cases, for there would be something definite, something determinate in the way in which they were dealt with. What happens now? The man goes through the mill again with his case, his eligibility is established, and he goes away quite satisfied that he is going to get his pension. Then within ten days he gets a notice, "Your pension is appealed." No reason is given for this action. I have taken up one or two cases and asked the reason for appealing them, but without getting any satisfaction. Apparently it is just a matter of routine. Does that occur in only a small proportion of these cases? No, I am told the appeals run as high as eighty per cent of the cases dealt with. There is the cause for dissatisfaction, that after going through two courts the returned man gets a letter saying, "Your case is appealed." He does not know on what grounds it is appealed, nor does the advocate. Every service man knows what a pension board is, and I would keep that title before him. I would change the system so that instead of a court sitting in camera you would have travelling pension boards. Then it is quite clear the number of appeals would be trifling. Our intention at the time the legislation was passed was that the man should have the benefit of this appeal court.

Hear, hear.

That was our thought in the
committee of 1930, that the court of appeal we had proposed would be for the benefit of the man. But now he has to go before a third court to fight his case. If the first two courts were pension courts, then of course there would be no appeal, and the appeal court would be what we intended it should be-a third place for the man to have his case reinstated. Let me add, Mr. Chairman, that the committee recommended and this parliament gave the men exactly what they wanted, but evidently some unseen, occult force has upset our plans. When we formed this court of appeal it was the intention that it would be for the benefit of the returned man.

Hear, hear.
Mr, ROSS:	Instead of that the Board of
Pension Commissioners have used it as a court of appeal to the extent of eighty per cent of the cases dealt with. That is the position we are in, and that is the difficulty. We should take the organization and say: "Here, work together, cooperate, coordinate and get this thing settled." I think, if anything, the county court judge would be the best man for the appeal court. I have no objection to the present courts of appeal. They have dealt fairly with any cases I have had before them. In several instances, as has been said, they felt there was further evidence that could be brought out, and instead of giving a decision they sent the case back to the tribunal. In that way I think the present head has shown his hearty sympathy for the returned man. All that is needed is a spirit of cooperation, a desire to work together; but a feeling of jealousy has crept into these courts, and as a result the returned man has suffered.

May I ask
the indulgence of the committee, Mr. Chairman, to refer to one other point? In doing so I may be crossing a bridge that may never be reached. It has been intimated to me that there is a move to change the legislation in this respect, that the tribunals which at present hear the cases and have power to adjudicate and render a decision are to have that power, withdrawn, and that travelling boards are to be constituted, boards of inquiry to gather the facts in relation to each application, and then to submit it to the Board of Pension Commissioners for decision. If that be so, I suggest to the minister that any step in that direction would be a .mistake. The whole trend of future legislation with a view to carrying out the wishes of those immediately concerned has been, instead of 
centralizing the matter of decisions in Ottawa, to decentralize as far as possible to the districts in which the men live. In the development of this legislation there have been brought into being the tribunals which sit in given centres and before which the applicants can bring their testimony and discuss their case with the members. The returned men have great confidence in this system and feel that they will obtain the best measure of justice by being face to face with the trial court which is to adjudicate upon their cases. There is a well grounded fear that if the power of adjudication is taken away from the tribunals and they be permitted to act only as fact finding bodies, the applicants will not obtain the treatment expected. I do not say that this action has been mooted by the government but it has been intimated to me on very good authority that it is under consideration, and I take this occasion of drawing to the attention of the minister that any step along this line would be considered as retrograde in character.

The fault does not lie with the organization, it lies with the authority which placed an almost impossible burden on the machinery. When the committee rose at six o'clock the minister was making some observations arising out of the discussion this afternoon. A few nights ago, when we were in supply on this item, I made some brief remarks and I want to repeat some of them. In my dealings with the minister he has always been very kind and patient, gone to a great deal of trouble and taken a personal interest in any matters I have brought before him, and I do not want him to think my remarks are at all critical. My only desire is that out of this discussion will come, if not this session-and I hope it will this session-perhaps next session some amendments to the Pension Act to overcome some of the difficulties and defects that have been found since the amendments have been added,
I have also nothing critical to say in regard to any official of the pension board, the tribunal, the appeal court or the department.
Mention was made this afternoon of the special committee that sat in 1930. I think the personnel of the committee of 1930 was practically the same as that of the committee of 1928, and most of the hon. members who spoke this afternoon were members of both those committees. In passing I should like to remark that the committee of 1928 and that of 1930, in recommending amendments to the Pension Act, made an earnest and sincere attempt to frame those amendments in the light of the evidence placed before them. This afternoon the hon. member for Kingston City mentioned the fact that almost everything the representatives of the legion and of other ex-service associations suggested, was carried out and embodied in the amendments made to the act in 1930. I think the greatest difficulty which the committee had at that time, and which appears to have been the bone of contention in regard to granting pensions ever since the inception of the act, that thousands of ex-service men had been discharged on demobilization without medical examination,' and that many had been discharged with a medical examination which was not very thorough, I do not lay the blame for this entirely on the authorities of that time, because when the men returned from overseas they were all anxious to get out of the service and back into civil life, and I believe many returned men at that time, for that reason, hesitated to say they had any disability. Those who were in charge of the administration of the act from the time of its
Supply-Pensions

inception to 1928 before the first committee was formed, and again up to 1930, were confronted with the situation that the great difficulty which lay in the way of a returned man receiving a pension was the fact that it was impossible for him or anyone else to prove absolutely that his disability, no matter of what sort it might be, was traceable to war service. The amendments were framed largely for the purpose of overcoming this problem so that the returned man, if he could not prove by medical authorities that his disability could be traced to war service, would get at least the benefit of the doubt and, if possible, a pension would be awarded to him.
From my observation of the working of the act since 1930 in connection with quite a number of cases that have come under my notice, I have reached the conclusion that the returned man does not always get the benefit of the doubt, as was intended under the amendments. In some cases it is perhaps more difficult now to prove that his disability can be traced to war service than it was before the amendments were added in 1930. If this objection could be overcome, I do not think there would be much criticism of the Pension Act. The trouble seems to me to be that we have too many boards or courts. We have first the Board of Pension Commissioners, second, the tribunals, and then the appeal court. In many instances where a returned man comes before a tribunal and the evidence is brought out, the verdict is that he is eligible for pension. He leaves thinking he has won his case and he is at last going to receive a pension. But that does not always happen; for the reason that the appeal court, which has not seen the man as the tribunal has, reviews the evidence and reverses the decision of the tribunal, the result being that the man who thought he had been granted a pension, does not receive it. That is a difficulty which should be removed, some method ought to be worked out whereby the intention of the amendments as added in 1930 in regard to giving the returned man the benefit of the doubt, may be made clearer and workable.
In connection with the act as it stands there are many other matters which in my opinion are not working out to the benefit of the exservice men. I well remember that in the committee of 1930 the hon. member for Kingston city took the stand-and I do not think he had any supporters; I am free to confess that I did not agree with him-that the whole machinery with regard to pensions would be clogged; that it would not work. As time has passed his judgment has proven

to be correct: there is a clogging of the machinery making it very difficult for the returned man to secure a pension. He may be out of work, as in many instances he is; he may have a wife and family depending upon him, and he is kept waiting for months and even years. I have in mind two cases that came under my observation, where the applications for pension were made before the Board of Pension Commissioners, one in September, 1930, and the other in November, 1930. In both cases the decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners was that the men were not entitled to pension. Both those cases were handed over to the tribunal, but they have not yet been heard and they go back to 1930. Surely that should not be. There should be some method whereby those cases could at least be heard and disposed of, favourably or otherwise, without that length of time elapsing. We have in, this country many men who have made applications for pensions and have been turned down, and that condition will continue to exist. Apart altogether from the justice of their cases, whether they are entitled to a pension or not, the whole machinery should be speeded up. I made that suggestion to the minister the other night, but from his remarks this afternoon I do not think that he took it seriously. The other night he gave the committee the number of cases that had come up, the number of cases pending, and other information in that regard. I know there is a tremendous number of cases pending, and thousands and thousands of cases which have not even come before the pension board yet. It is a well known fact that many men returned from overseas apparently physically fit, but as the months and years went on, some disability developed which they claim is due to their war service. That condition will continue, and if there is any way in which the minister and his department and the government can work out some amendments to the act to accelerate the machinery, I think I can assure him that if those amendments are brought down even this session he will receive the most sympathetic cooperation from this side of the house.
I would appeal to the minister to take into consideration, I will not say the criticism, but the suggestions that have been made this afternoon in regard to the working out of the Pension Act. I know that the minister is sympathetic. I know that he has a very heavy department to administer and that at times it may be difficult to satisfy the claims of returned men, but if he would give this matter some attention, I think with his offi-

cials he would be able to work out some solution which would improve the condition that now exists.
The hon. member for Kingston this afternoon mentioned another matter. He thought that there was not the proper cooperation and coordination between the pension board, the tribunal, and the appeal court, and he mentioned especially the lack of cooperation as between the tribunal and the appeal court. It may be so. I have no knowledge of this, but the hon. member for Kingston as a rule speaks of things of which he has full knowledge, and he must have some information which bears out the remarks he made this afternoon. No hon. member who sat in this house three or four years ago will deny that at one time there was a lack of cooperation and coordination between the pension board and the appeal board of that day. That was proven, I think, before the special committee on pensions that sat in the session of 1928. This is a matter which should receive the attention of the minister, and if it is one of the difficulties that is keeping ex-service men waiting, not only for months but for years, to get a hearing, the minister should take action to remedy it without delay. I feel satisfied that he will, and that he will be able to work out some solution of this very difficult problem. It is a problem that has grown with the years and will continue to grow. I do not think that this country will be able to reduce to any material extent its expenditure on military pensions for the next fifteen or twenty or perhaps thirty years. My own opinion is that the number of applications and the expenditure for pensions will continue to increase.
The suggestion was made this afternoon by some hon. members that a solution of the difficulty might be to have the county court judges hear the pension cases. They may be right, but I do not think so. I am not in favour of that suggestion. I do not think the county court judges should be asked to take up this work. I think rather it should be done along the present lines, but the difficulties that now exist should be smoothed out.
I will mention a matter on which I dwelt for a moment or two the other night. The travelling tribunals when they visit certain places to hear cases do not clear up all the cases they have on their docket. Notices are sent out to returned men that their applications for pension will be heard at a certain place on a certain date, and they travel perhaps many miles to get to that place with the expectation that at least their cases will be heard. But the cases are not all heard. There may be ten or twelve cases on the
docket and only three or four or five may be heard, and the men whose cases are not heard have to go back home without even knowing when they will have another chance to have their cases heard.

I remember that the hon. member for Kingston made a proposal which, in the newspapers, was called the Ross scheme; the other was called the Power scheme, because it was introduced by the chairman of the committee. Considering that immense amount of money, it is well to remember that the total national revenue of Canada before the year 1900 never amounted to

$50,000,000. I mention that fact merely to indicate the immensity of the undertaking before us. It is not always as easy to deal with a question as one might believe. I think the hon. member for Muskoka has said, and the statement has been made this afternoon on several occasions, that 30,000 cases are awaiting attention. I am informed by the officers now sitting in front of the minister that the number is only 23,900, and that includes cases which are not at all serious. There is no use making the condition any worse than it really is. I am informed by one of the officers in front of me that a few days ago a soldier who had served only one day applied for a pension.
Although mentioning these facts, I am not trying to indicate that there is no room for improvement; we all know there is. Last year we made improvements, and they had been made before; but it seems to me we shall be making a mistake if from year to year we continue to change the act. I mention these facts as one who was a member of the old committee. I believe my hon. friend from South Perth served at that time, but I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was in the house then. Certainly all parties in the house put forth an endeavour to satisfy the soldiers to the greatest possible extent.
I quite agree with my hon. friend.
Probably we went the absolute limit, because hon. members will recall that an election was at hand, and all parties were anxious to give satisfaction.
I quite agree with the minister.

I cannot let the minister get away with that. May I say that I pride myself in the accuracy of my statements. Although I have sat in this house a good many years I never had to withdraw any statement I had made. Irrespective of what the officials have told the minister, I must say that the figures I am about to give came to me a few days ago from the secretary of the Board of Pension Commissioners. Although I have given them to the committee already, I feel I must now repeat them. The number of applications on hand by the Board of Pension Commissioners on February 29, 1932, was 23,900. On the same date there were 2,650 applications before the pension tribunals, and before the appeal court there were 1,316. If those figures are incorrect I cannot be blamed; I took the time from their clock-

they gave it to me. Those figures were supplied Iby the Board of Pension Commissioners, and I submit, sir, that we should take as correct the figures we get from officials of this department. I know the gentlemen sitting in front of the minister dispute my figures, but with all due respect to them I think statistics supplied by the Board of Pension Commissioners are more reliable than statistics supplied by them.

I have asked the officers of the department now sitting in front of the minister, and they adhere to the figure of 23,900. They say, however, that there are a number of cases now being dealt with by the aippeal 'boards which are not included in that figure.

Mr. Chairman, I do not regard this discussion as being in any way a waste of time. I think the joint intention of hon. members who have participated in this discussion is, if possible, to improve the administration of the pension scheme. One of the finest notes in the whole discussion is that not the slightest tinge of partisanship has 'been displayed by any hon. member who has spoken.
The hon. member for Kingston to-day gave a very able resume of the history of the pension legislation in the Dominion of Canada. Many hon. members in this house will recall the first struggle which took place in the years 1919 and 1920 through the organized veterans' organizations to have important amendments made to the pension legislation. They will recall the work that was done by parliamentary committees sitting from year to year. Finally, as a result of recommendations made by a parliamentary committee a royal commission presided over by my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth was appointed. That commission went throughout Canada and heard evidence. As a result of their report legislation was passed to form the federal appeal board, and a system of soldiers' advocates. That system was not considered to operate as people thought it would, and in 1930, as the result of the work of a committee of that year, the present act was brought into effect.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said this afternoon that there were two flaws in the present administration. I agreed with him as far as he went. I am convinced of one thing, that the first defect in the present administration resulted from the amendment passed in 1931. That amendment was ex. cellent, to a certain degree, and will, in time, operate to the benefit of ex-service men and
the nation. The flaw in it, however, in my opinion is that it has placed upon the Board of Pension Commissioners a task which they cannot efficiently carry out. I am convinced, from personal observations, that to-day the pension board is trying to carry out a task which is really beyond its powers. The first remedy-and I am speaking in the most friendly way to the minister-if we are to keep in force the amendment of 1931, is if possible to enlarge the Board of Pension Commissioners so as not to have the system glutted at the outset.
The other evening I spoke about the pension tribunals, and so far as my observations have gone I must say these gentlemen have carried out their duties in a most exemplary manner. As far as the province of British Columbia is concerned-and this part of my remarks might possibly be political-I have nothing but commendation for the minister because of his choice of the two distinguished gentlemen he has appointed from our province to carry out the work of the pension tribunals. I do not believe that in the entire province you could find two gentlemen who are better qualified for carrying out this very important work. If the personnel throughout the rest of Canada is of the same standard it is of a very high order indeed.
This afternoon the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray), complained that the tribunals did not visit the small centres. My hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) suggested in a very constructive sense indeed that some of the powers for the secondary review might very well be bestowed on the county court judges. This, I think, is well worth consideration by the minister. For some fifteen or sixteen months we have trained twelve able officers of the pension tribunal. By their decisions, some of which have been upset by the appeal court, they must now have a very intimate knowledge of the Pension Act, and I believe they are thoroughly competent to deal impartially with any cases which may be brought before them, and that they will give the returned soldier the benefit of the doubt without imperilling in any appreciable degree the security of the treasury. I have always had the suspicion that the ultimate tribunal is inclined to be influenced by too careful consideration for the security of the treasury as against the merits of the case affecting the returned soldier.
I wish to object most strenuously to the system of commission counsel. I believe the officers of the pension tribunals can be de-

pended upon to render a fair and impartial verdict in regard to every service case that comes before them. Now the minister has got twelve men trained in this work, and he might very well allow each one to form a pension tribunal. This would give him twelve courts instead of four, which would go some distance towards meeting the point made by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and the hon. member for West Lambton.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
We have six divisions

Then he could have two apiece for each court. That would enable the smaller centres to be visited, and the grievance in this respect would be immediately remedied.
My experience is that the main grievance of the ex-servicemen to-day is twofold. In the first instance, there is the delay in dealing with the case of the successful appellant which has been appealed from the pension tribunal to the appeal court of Ottawa. In the second place, there is the system of having a commission counsel lodge an appeal against the successful pension applicant. I think it absolutely contrary to all the accepted canons of justice and equity that an official under the direction of the Board of Pension Commissioners, the court of first instance, should himself direct the appeal from the decision of the gentlemen of the pension tribunal-who have seen the applicant and, as was said by an hon. member this afternoon, have studied his demeanour and have heard all the evidence- to a body down here who can only refer to the record of the case. As I say, I am convinced that even if your tribunals to-day were your ultimate court in regard to pensions, the treasury would not suffer to any appreciable degree. Then there is the delay here in Ottawa after the successful applicant has his appeal launched by the pension advocate. You have the machinery clogged throughout the three stages. I urge the minister to enlarge the personnel of the board as I have suggested, which he could do without incurring extra expense. I may tell him that they are far more sympathetic towards the cause of the returned soldier than they were nine or ten years ago. That may be due to the threat of appeal machinery hanging over their heads. If you enlarge the machinery of your court of first instance, if you make one member of the pension tribunal a quorum to hear appeals in the country, and if you take away from the commission counsel the power of launching appeals in the appeal court, I am 
convinced that the thirty thousand cases to which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario referred will be disposed of within eight or ten months, with resultant satisfaction to the many ex-servicemen throughout the dominion.

Has the minister any information as to whether the Board of Pension Commissioners in the past have used detective agencies for the purpose of securing information about applicants for pensions prior to the time of their enlistment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have no knowledge on that point. I do not know that I thoroughly follow what the hon. member is asking.
Perhaps the minister will allow me to answer. There have always been what are known as social service investigators, who do make investigations with respect to the applicant's family history.
Has it been the practice of the pension board to employ detective agencies for the purpose of obtaining information with regard to the applicant for a pension prior to the time of his enlistment?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I cannot say as to employing detective agencies, but I can quite understand the pension board would investigate the early history of an applicant for pension whenever they thought it necessary. The early medical history might have a very direct bearing upon the man's disability.

Would it be necessary, for instance, in the case of a man claiming a pension for an injured arm or hand to make such an investigation? I can quite understand that in cases of certain diseases such an investigation might be necessary, but not for a physical injury.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I would say it might be necessary to ascertain whether the loss occurred previous to enlistment or not.
The man could not enlist if he had lost an arm or a hand.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, the minister must have a lapse of memory. A layman's opinion with respect to a man's sight previous to enlistment would be absolutely worthless.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

I had a case brought
to my attention the other day which seemed to me to be rather extravagant. The Thiel Detective Agency of Montreal was engaged to find out something about the applicant prior to enlistment. In this man's file there is a report signed by T. A. Lawson, acting general manager of the Thiel Detective Agency. The person whose history was to be investigated, the man who was applying for pension, had an injured left hand, and the board had supplied him with certain casings to put over that hand. The investigator began his work on April 2, 1924. He left Ottawa, went to Toronto and then to Collingwood, and came back to Ottawa again. On May 14 he went to Regina, then to Moose Jaw, then to Caron, back to Moose Jaw, again to Regina, then to Prince Albert, to Shell Brook, then back to Moose Jaw, to Mossbank, then to Cranbrook, British Columbia, to Fernie and finally back to Ottawa, arriving here on June 6. When the matter was brought to my attention it did seem to me that the Board of Pension Commissioners must have been pretty hard up to find an excuse to avoid paying a pension to a man whose hand was injured through war service.	.
