Since the matter has been
introduced I should like to say a word or two on this question of investigators. I have no objection to the ordinary investigator who goes around and asks a man about his occupation, his ability to work, or his income, or who asks the man's employer these questions, but I do not like the way some of these men do their work. As my hon. friend from Acadia has mentioned, the department does not hesitate to spend quite large sums of money in investigations of this kind, and I know of one case in which an investigation was carried out in the old country and brought 41761-114
forth evidence trying to show that a certain injury had been caused eleven or twelve years before the time alleged.
I do object to the procedure followed in one case which came to my knowledge. The question largely turned upon whether or not the man was deaf previous to a certain occasion, and one of these industrial investigators, or whatever they call them, was sent around to make an inquiry. He did not go near the man; he did not tell the man he was making this investigation, nor did he tell the people whom he interviewed that his inquiry was of vital importance to the man in question. I will not say he snooped around, although that word was used; I suppose he was carrying out his duties to the best of his ability. He would go to a little town; he would go to the grocery store and ask the proprietor, "Do you know John Smith"? The answer would be yes, and then he would ask, "Is he deaf"? The storekeeper would answer, "I do not know; I never noticed it. I do not think so." That would go into the record, and that was the procedure followed right along. The investigator did not tell the persons he interviewed how important the matter was to the soldier; the soldier himself had no opportunity of hearing this evidence, but when the matter came up for decision that man lost his case largely because there were several foolscap pages of evidence of a similar kind. I was told that if I were given an opportunity of seeing this damning evidence I would not have been dissatisfied with the decision of the court, but I put this to the minister: If this man had been accused of a crime would evidence obtained in that way have been used against him? Of course it would not. The people would have been sworn and they would have been confronted with the accused. But because he was a soldier asking for a pension, that sort of evidence was accepted. Surely that is carrying this investigating business too far. I objected at the time and I still object. If we are to have these courts, with two government counsel against one counsel for the soldier, surely the inquiry should be conducted in a legal way and evidence which is not given under oath should not be accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
May I correct my hon. friend in his statement that two government counsel are employed as against one for the soldier? That statement has been made before, but it is not so. Two government counsel do not appear as against one advocate for the soldier.

I am glad to hear the minister say he would like particulars of these furnished to him, but I ask him now what good it will do. I have a case that was turned down by the court of appeal; I think judgment was signed by Judge Hyndman. The man has a cardiac condition, with rheumatism and arthritis, and he is absolutely incapable of doing anything to-day. It was absolutely proved that his condition was due to war service, but in their investigations they got a positive reaction to a Kahn test for syphilis, and on that ground Judge Hyndman signed judgment depriving this man of his pension. That test is not specific; any medical man knows it is not definite. You will get it in connection with many other diseases. This soldier was a respectable man; he absolutely denied ever having had that disease, but even if that had been true it could have had nothing to do with his disability. The judgment was absolutely absurd and ridiculous to any man with any knowledge of medicine, and through that judgment this man lost his pension. I do not hesitate to say that I could submit that evidence to one hundred medical men, and that one hundred per cent of them would say he was unjustly deprived of his pension, but what recourse has he? If I give the minister the evidence will he say that he will correct this injustice?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Would you repeat your question?
If I submit the evidence to the minister will he correct this injustice?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
This gives me an opportunity to say a word to many hon. members who perhaps do not fully understand the working of these courts. I have nothing to do with the pension board; it is my duty to allow that board to form its own judgments without interference, especially as the minister could not possibly know all the circumstances of the case. That is also true with regard to the tribunal and the appeal court. In a

judicial way these bodies are independent of the minister, as they should be, and so I take that attitude. What I said to my hon. friend the leader of the Progressive party was that I should lay the files and the information before him. It does not follow that I am going to express any opinion on any particular case, but I will assist any hon. member to the best of my ability.

I think the minister is quite right, and I never thought anything else, but his remark might have caused some misunderstanding. The point I am trying to make is this: We have a final court of appeal which has given a judgment which is absolutely absurd and which has deprived a man of what is rightfully his. What recourse is left to that man? He won his case before the tribunal when he proved that his disability was due to the war. That was accepted by the court of appeal, but they deprived him of any benefits because in performing a routine test they obtained a positive reaction for syphilis-a reaction on a test which is not specific .and final and which is obtained in many other diseases. And the man absolutely and positively denied having this particular infection. There is a case of rank injustice. The judgment was signed by Judge Hyndman of the court of appeal. Now the man is down and out and cannot earn a dollar; he is a cripple.
Under the meritorio.ua clause, how many cases have been submitted to the Board of Pension Commissioners since the amendments of 1930, and in how many of them has decision been rendered?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am afraid I have not the numbers here; I believe I stated that there were thirty-seven applications and one hearing.

As a
matter of fact, there were forty-seven applications, roughly speaking, and so far only in one case has decision been given. Surely that is an absolute outrage after eighteen months; in that time decision should have been rendered one way or the other. I know of applications that have been made from all over Canada to the Board of Pension Commissioners, and only one judgment has so far been rendered under this clause. I cannot conceive the reason for this delay. These are the most urgent cases of all, as a rule.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a complaint made to me by several applicants for pension who have been ordered to report to Belcher hospital for examination. In one instance the applicant

had a bad heart. He was engaged in manual labour, and when he complained he was taken to Belcher hospital, put to bed and taken care of for about a month before the examination was made. If this is the practice that is to be carried out, then I submit that these men have very just grounds for complaint. It is obvious that in most cases a heart affection improves after the patient has been in bed for some time under proper care, and if the returned soldier is to be examined for heart trouble he should be examined the moment he comes in from the country, for that is the time when his heart is bothering him. I know nothing about medicine but I do submit in all fairness that that is the proper time to have the medical examination. After the man has been in bed a month under proper treatment it is highly probable that the doctors will report his heart as normal; then he goes back to work and after a short interval his heart begins to bother him again and interferes with his work. This is one practice which the minister could rectify; he could see to it that when men are sent for examination the examination is made at once. The doctors should see the man under the conditions in which he has to work ordinarily. Will the minister undertake to have the present practice changed?

I shall be pleased to

I did not get the minister's
reply to the point I raised. I can assure him that there are several men who have told [DOT] me that what I have stated has actually taken place so far as they are cornicerned. speechtext: If the hon. member will let me have the names, I shall have the matter promptly investigated and let him know. I think, however, it is fair to hear all the facts first.

I can give the minister a history of a case that occurred long before his time. This was a mam in my own neighbourhood, a young chap who came back from overseas with some weakness that caused him to have fainting fits when under heavy work, so that he could not carry on his ordinary job. He looked as fit as a fiddje when he was resting, but he could not do any work; his heart bothered him. I knew nothing about his heart, but at my solicitation he was sent to hospital three times for examination. The facts as I am giving them were confirmed by 'the doctor. The man was put under observation in a state of absolute quietude, and he remained in bed for some time. While in bed his heart behaved normally-it always did when it was in bed. I complained; I said [DOT]that, though I was a layman, I did not think it was common sense to examine him under such conditions. I suggested that he should be examined under conditions in which he usually showed his symptoms. Finally, in order to get rid of me, thinking me a nuisance, they said "We will give you authority to have him examined under whatever conditions you suggest." I had him put through a physical test for two or three minutes and immediately his heart action was affected. That was what they said. I can assure the minister of this case because I accompanied the man on each occasion in order that I could verify what he said.
Before six o'clock the minister made three statements, or rather one statement that might be divided into 'three parts. First, he commented on the difference of opinion among

the members and spoke of the consequent difficulty of arriving at any conclusion from what they said. My own observation was that there was unusual unanimity on the part of hon. members as to the best method to be tested out. The minister then said, quite correctly, that the situation which existed was no fault of the different boards, the Board of Pension Commissioners, or the tribunals, or the appeal court, but was the fault of the committee of which I had been a member as well as himself, we had imposed on these bodies an impossible task which we expected them to perform. But unfortunately the minister concluded with the statement that the situation was not so bad, that the boards were keeping up with their work fairly well, and that there was not so much cause for alarm. Some of us may have disagreed somewhat in the committee itself, but as one of those who agreed to a unanimous report, I am prepared-and I suggest there are others- to rectify a mistake which the minister says we made, in order to take these men away from the impossible position in which the minister suggests they are placed, and to take from them that impossible load which the minister indicates we have placed upon their shoulders.

Some years ago the Alberta legislature decided to offer government house for sale. There were no offers to buy the house, whereupon it was restored as the residence of the lieutenant-governor. As a final word I should

I regret I have
not been present during the entire discussion on this matter, but I should like to make a few observations regarding the operation of the Pension Act. I understand this legislation was brought into existence with the unanimous assent of the house, and that it is not looked upon as a party measure. Nevertheless, almost every one of us realizes that there is a great defect in administration and I want to point out one defect which I think exists in the law and should be remedied. I do not wish to coin a startling phrase, but I really believe the returned soldier, who is an applicant for a pension, is under our legislation treated in a worse way than a man who is charged in our courts with an ordinary crime, and I think I can prove what I say. When a man is charged in our courts with a crime and the court of first instance renders judgment in bis favour, a judgment of not guilty, the crown has no appeal; the only appeal it has is against sentence. What is the situation that we find under the pension law? I understand the cardinal principle in the act was that a returned man, an applicant for pension, ought to have the benefit of the doubt; that is one principle that has been enshrined in our legislation. What happens? By law he has in the first instance the benefit of the doubt. He goes before the tribunal and a declaratory judgment is passed in his favour. That is, his case passes altogether from the region of doubt and partakes of the nature of a positive judgment. Then what happens? The crown appeals the case. After

S upply-Pensions
that what is the mental attitude of a returned man towards his country? A competent tribunal has passed a declaratory judgment that he is entitled to a pension and the court of appeal wipes out that judgment altogether and claims that he is not so entitled. Therefore when I make the statement that under out present legislation an applicant for pension is treated less fairly than a man charged with a crime, I think it goes without argument that such is the case.
I believe the legislation might be remedied in this way: * I understand the returned men asked for this court of appeal in order to protect their rights. This country, once a judgment is passed by the tribunal in favour of a pensioner, ought to stand by that decision, and the right of the erowm to appeal should be wiped out of the statute.
I should like to refer to the matter of congestion which exists at present in regard to the hearing of applications for pension. If that congestion is not removed before long, it is certainly going to be disastrous to this parliament and government at the next election. I know the returned men are becoming absolutely dissatisfied; they are wondering what is happening. I should like to make this suggestion by way of an improvement in the existing legislation. Recently we had a debate in the house about the salaries paid to our judges, and I think it was indicated that we have in our population of 10,000,000, more judges than they have in Great Britain and Ireland with a population of 45,000,000. I am not in favour of reducing judges' salaries, but that is another matter; I am in favour of giving the judges more work. I would suggest that the county court judges, in order to get this congestion cleared up, might have equal power with the pension tribunal and for that matter we might give to the service of the returned soldier applicants for pension, two weeks of the long vacation and possibly the first week of the ensuing court session. I make these observations in all sincerity, as a returned soldier, and also at the suggestion of the combined returned soldiers' organizations of the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
I should like to ask the minister whether he has decided to take his tubercular cases away from Calydor sanatorium?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The answer is no, I have not decided. I think there will not be many going.

Then that compels me
to make a few observations, Mr. Chairman, and I predicate them upon this, that parliament and the government should keep faith. When they cease to do that, we are in a deplorable condition. That necessitates my going back for about ten or twelve years when a parliamentary committee of this house on pensions requested the government of the day to make an agreement with Calydor sanatorium in the district of Muskoka for taking care of the tubercular patients who are wards of the government. The committee made that request because this institution is one of the best in Canada or on the continent of America, and because they were not able to use it to the extent that they wanted to use it. At that time there were many thousands of patients nominally listed as tubercular but in whose case the final diagnosis had not been made, and consequently they were not drawing a pension. The object of the request was that this institution should be used to make a final diagnosis and clear up these cases in order that they might be properly treated and that those who were illegally drawing full-time pensions should not be allowed to draw them. The people of (hat institution agreed to the request of the government, and they put up three dollars to every one that the government of the day put up. They increased their staff and overhead expenses, and they have never got the patients to which they were entitled according to the agreement. As a result the overhead and cost of maintenance for the patients was increased even for civilians, and to-day that institution is in financial distress. Probabfy I should not say that but it is a fact, due to the agreement which they made with the government of this country. They lived up to the letter and spirit of the agreement, but the country did not. The institution never got the patients that they were legitimately entitled to expect, although I do not believe that any number was definitely specified in the agreement.
I ain informed by the medical superintendent, Mr. Chairman, that the other day this institution got a letter from the department that it was going to close the whole thing out, going to scrap that institution and leave it with that increased staff and increased overhead expenses. The surprising thing to me is this, that when I spoke to the minister about it he did not know anything about it although the letter that was received by the institution said that the matter was finally settled. Now the question I want to ask the
Supply-Pensions

minister is this: Who is running his department? Are the officials going to decide and settle matters of policy and give final judgment without the minister knowing anything about it? If I were minister and an official did that for me he would lose his job the next morning. It is a most humiliating position for officials in a department to decide and settle matters of policy and notify those concerned that that is the end of it without the minister himself knowing anything about it. Over and above that, the point I want to impress on the committee is this, that parliament and the government of the day solicited the agreement with that institution; it was recommended by the pension committee of that day, and the government of the day made the agreement. The institution lived up to the spirit and the letter of the agreement, and as a consequence they have suffered serious financial loss. What I want to ask the minister is this: Is he going to repudiate the spirit of that agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: So far as that question goes, I do not .propose to answer any question suggesting that the minister .is going to repudiate anything. I would ask the minister to be a little more definite and say wherein I mistated the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is very easy. The member stated that I did not know that notice had (been sent. I did know it. It was proposed that they continue on the same basis as other sanatoria.
All I have to say, and I will apologize if I am wrong, is that when I went in to discuss it with the minister he did not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Excuse me, I did.
. Mr. McGIBBON: The minister said he did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

Unemployment relief, $1,250,000.
Who are eligible under that vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Pensioners who are in need of help, bearing in mind the pensions they are receiving and other means at their disposal. The other day the vote was increased to the extent of $875,000. Last year the vote was $1,250,000, but in the supplementary estimates of two or three days ago an increase of $875,000 was made. During the last year relief was administered during the summer months, a procedure which is not customary. Then, there were more applicants, and the municipalities now direct the men to the department rather than find work for them locally. For those reasons there are more calls on the resources of the department.

Is a
pensioner eligible, no matter what the assessment of his pension may be?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He is, if it is a small assessment. If it is sufficiently high he does not receive money from this vote.
Is there a fixed percentage?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, he could not depend on the pension. If he received a full pension he would not come under this vote, because his pension would be sufficient. If, however, he received only a small pension his receipts might be brought up to a certain figure.

What relief can be given to a returned soldier who has applied for a pension, whose case is not decided and who is unable to work or to find work? I understand that no relief is given in such cases, and am wondering if it is not possible to make provision for them. I have in mind two instances where applications have been brought 'before the pensions 'board, and in both cases not only are they unable to find work, but if they could find it they would not be able to take it because of their incapacity. These men are literally at the
mercy of their friends and neighbours. Both are married, and one has a family of six children. Surely in cases of that kind something should be done, although there may be no authority under the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The cases described by my hon. friend would come under the civil unemployment relief, but not under the present vote.

When there is no work for them, what must they do? Are they to starve in the meantime? So far as I know there has been no direct relief provided. There are numerous cases throughout the country such as I have described, although I cite only two from my own county. Perhaps the minister would consult with his officials and see if during the winter months some relief could be afforded. Fifteen or twenty dollars a month would be very helpful in the winter time.

Could the minister tell us if this money is actually being spent? I ask the question because I have received communications from two merchants to the effect that these moneys have not gone forward to the needy people.

speechtext: The relief is not tendered in cash, but orders for groceries and coal are given. Cheques are sent to householders to pay rent bills.

speechtext:
My hon. friend will
understand that those payments had to await passage of the supplementary vote for $875,000, and the royal assent, which was not obtained until a short time later. Cheques have gone out.
How many in the three maritime provinces received relief under this vote ?

speechtext:
If the hon. member
wishes I shall send that information to him; I do not have it before me.

Will the back amounts be paid in cases where assistance has not been given since January? As I understand it, the exservice man cannot get this relief unless his pension is low. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I would not wish to encourage my hon. friend. The building was destroyed. About twenty-five men were engaged there. As a matter of fact these factories have passed their original objective, which was to train the men, not to give them employment for the remainder of their active days. But these factories have been continued, although there is some discontent among those for whom we cannot find room in them. While these factories do give complete relief to the men who are able to get into them, still I do not think it would be in the general interest to acquire more factories.
How many are employed in the four shops still in existence?

So it costs $70,000 a year to look after those one hundred and ninety men?

They are earning their
living in those factories. This is a better way of helping them than the method suggested by my hon. friend.
Would not the same argument apply equally as well to those returned men in Winnipeg who to-day are doing practically nothing on account of the shop having been burned down?

Item agreed to.
Grant to Last Post Fund, $35,000.

I am heartily in sympathy

There seems to be considerable dissatisfaction, Mr. Chairman, in the working of this tribunal. After the pension tribunal has met the applicant personally, gone into all the details of his case, and decided in his favour, I think it is most unfair that an appeal should be taken by an official of the department, with the result that in many cases the successful applicant before the pension tribunal is deprived of his pension. I think this should be looked into, and I should like to hear what the minister has to say on the subject.

War veterans' allowances, $1,300,000.

As this represents a cut of

Supply-National Health
but up to the present the administration has been satisfactorily conducted. speechtext: This item is an unavoidable expenditure. If the men are qualified I presume they will be paid no matter what may be the estimate. This is one of the most satisfactory parts of our pension work.

year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext:
May I
point out that up to September 1, 1931, when the legislation had been in force for one year, the number of those receiving allowances was 3,019, representing an expenditure of $990,084. That was the first year.
Then it is quite possible that the amount provided in the estimates will be sufficient for the ensuing year.

I should
like to quote just one other paragraph from the annual report of the department:
The work is up to date in so far that on December 1, 1931, 8.490 applications had been received by the committee, of which 8.375 had been finally disposed of; the remaining 115 having been deferred for further information or awaiting consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am very glad these

National Health

quarantine: salaries and contingencies of organized districts, public health in other districts, Tracadie and Bentinck Island lazarettoes and leprosy generally, $192,000.

and the lepers removed to the quarantine station in Quebec. At that time the minister assured me that nothing had been heard of it in the department for at least the last year and a half. how many doctors are engaged in this work abroad?

speechtext:
It is necessary to have

I thought we were not
permitting any immigration from the continent. If that is so, why keep medical inspectors over there?

Item agreed to.
Supply-National Health
Grant to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, $18,000.

I should like to know why
this item is being reduced by $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is the ten per cent
reduction.

Is it the intention to pay
the blind a smaller pension this year? This is about the last place we should start to curtail our expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If the hon. member will look over the grants he will find them all treated in the same way.

I do not think these blind
people ever received sufficient pension, and I protest against the action of the government in making this reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This is not for pensions to the blind. It is a grant.

Surely the government are not going to cut the blind as well as those who can see. They are going a long way when they reduce by $2,000 the grant to the Institute for the Blind. I had thought that before now they would have revised the old age pension scheme so as to take care of the blind under that provision. Had a real government been returned to power, the blind would have been receiving assistance to-day under the old age pensions legislation. Surely this is one place where the government should have refrained from putting their knife into the allowance made to suffering humanity-an allowance of $20,000. The matter is wmrthy of reconsideration.

In connection with this grant to the institute for the blind, may I say that during the last campaign I was asked whether I was in favour of pensions for the blind, and I said I was. Probably, therefore, it would be consistent for me now to repeat that statement here. I am not going to make a speech, but I wish to call the matter to the attention of the minister. It seems to me that if this parliament can legislate on pensions because of the disability of age, by the same token they have power to pass legislation to meet the disability of lack of sight. The age set under the Old Age Pension Act is three score years and ten. That age is fixed because it has been found that after seventy years of age a person who is without means of supporting himself is helpless. The basis of the pension is the physical inability of the individual to make his way in this world. Age is one disability and lack of sight is another, and if blindness comes before the

age of seventy it is a disability that prevents the individual from earning his living. I urge that upon the minister. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River suggested that if a real government were in power they might do something about it. In reply to the hon. gentleman I would point out that in 1926, I placed on the order paper-and this was when a government which was supposed to be a real government was in power-this question:
Is it the intention of the federal government to introduce legislation to provide pensions for the blind?
The answer I received, which is of record, as given by the then Prime Minister, now leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), was:
The matter of pensions for the blind is not enumerated under the provisions in the British North America Act applying exclusively to the dominion.
That was the stand taken by the party supported by the hon. member. But apart altogether from that, I think the principle is sound, and I hope to see the day when, whether it be by an amendment to the old age pensions legislation, or by a separate act, legislation will be introduced in this house making the matter of pensions for the blind a federal burden to be dealt with by Canada as a whole, so that those afflicted people will get similar treatment throughout the dominion.

Will the
minister give some details of the expenditures under this item? What is the work done by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind? How many persons do they care for?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The institute was formed by the combination of existing organizations in Canada and it works in close affiliation with similar local bodies. The total expenses incurred exceed $200,000 per annum, which is raised from grants from the federal, provincial and municipal authorities, and from private subscriptions. Industrial establishments are maintained at Halifax, Ottawa, Toronto and Winnipeg. There was authorized in 1919 payment of an annual grant of $10,000 for a period of five years.

I doubt
whether during the last nine years there has been a single session when some hon. gentleman somewhere in the house has not asked that this item be increased rather than decreased. The necessity for caring for unfortunate people so afflicted touches a keen chord of human sympathy, and I think this

Supply-National Health
should be one of the last departments to be affected, if ever it is affected, by the so-called economy program of the government. I join with those who have preceded me in protesting against this reduction. There are one or two other items in which reductions are equally inexcusable, but this one certainly will not receive the approval of the Canadian public. Any reduction in a vote intended to take care of acute human suffering or of a disability of this type will be protested against all over Canada.

I wish to say one word in support of the attitude that has been taken towards this reduction. In protesting against it I would point out something that perhaps is not apparent to everyone. At this time, during a year when able-bodied men, in full possession of all their faculties, find it unusually difficult to secure employment to support themselves and their families, it becomes doubly and trebly difficult for people who are afflicted with any major disability, and particularly blindness, to obtain work. These people are placed at a peculiar disadvantage at this time when competition for any position at all is so keen. All positions to-day are eagerh' sought by men in full possession of all their faculties, and under these circumstances the condition of the blind becomes very much accentuated. I would protest against the reduction. I think that public opinion, to say nothing of the opinion in the house on all sides, would certainly have supported a substantial increase in such an item rather than a decrease. May I also support the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, a suggestion which has been discussed in this house from time to time but never dealt with; I refer to the question of pensions for the blind. The blind form a class set apart from all others; their situation is so peculiar that pensions granted to them would not arouse jealousy among other people. It would not establish a precedent whereby others suffering from other infirmities might come forward and demand similar consideration. This disability forces people to move in a world of darkness all the days of their life, and to people so afflicted generous treatment should be given. Such treatment, I say, would not be resented by others nor would it constitute a precedent; on the contrary, it would be appreciated and supported by the whole country. Another factor must be considered, namely, the extent of such assistance; I do not mean individual assistance, but the total cost. After all, and most fortunately, this is a class comparatively limited in numbers and the total cost would
not be such as to prohibit reasonably sympathetic consideration of their case. I hope that at some time, and the sooner the better, the house will have the pleasure of supporting a measure which will provide, on the part of the people of this country, financial assistance for the blind.

May I point out to my hon. friend that in past years this grant has not been so large as it is this year? The grant started originally in 1919 at $10,000 and for a number of years continued at that figure. In 1921-22 it was raised to $20,000 and in 1924-25 and continuing years it was dropped again to $10,000. Then in 1928-29 it was raised to $15,000 and it has been $20,000 for only a couple of years. No one questions the sympathy to which my hon. friend and the other hon. gentleman have given expression in regard to people who are blind, but the fact is that it was thought the easiest way to deal with all these grants was, if there were to be any cuts at all, rather than cut out some entirely, to make a ten per cent cut in all of them, and this has been done. In view of the past amount of the grant, I think that is the fairest method that could be adopted. I am not quarrelling with the statement made by anybody in regard to the sympathy these people deserve, but at the same time this seems a fair action when one remembers the grant was $10,000 only a few years ago.

The remarks of the
Minister of Railways afford me an opportunity for making another protest. I think there is some justice in his contention that it is better to reduce all the grants by a certain percentage than to eliminate some entirely, but I notice one grant is eliminated, that to the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, an organization which has done splendid work throughout the whole country, the value of which can hardly be estimated, work of an educational character which, if we consider the fact that every year brings a fresh contingent of young people who arrive at the age when such education is necessary, must be carried on continuously if it is to be of anj' value. May I suggest that it would be well for the future of Canada, well for the future of the entire community, if the suggestion made by the Minister of Railways were carried out completely and none of these grants, particularly that of the nature I have indicated, were cut out.

tion only, because, if I remember aright, I do not think he was a member of the last parliament-
I said 1926.

I am speaking of 1926 to 1930. The hon. member stated that he placed a question on the order paper in 1926, asking whether it was the intention of the government to introduce legislation to provide pensions for the blind, and the then prime minister, now leader of the opposition, answered to the effect that the matter came within the jurisdiction, not of the federal parliament but rather of the provinces. The situation is this, that this being a matter that did come and still comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces, we had representations made to us by various provinces that the first time the Old Age Pension Act was amended we should take care of the blind. The blind people in 1928 or 1929, I am not sure which, had the assurance-I was on the delegation that met them -that the first time we amended the Old Age Pension Act they would be taken care of under it, of course with consent of the provinces. The act was amended last session and the representation was made across the floor of the house to the present government, but they did not see fit to accede to it. That is why I made the remark I did.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy river for explaining once more that this is one of the many things which the party he supports would have done had they remained in power.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene, $9,000.

This appropriation is not cut just ten per cent and the Minister of Railways should explain why the tip of the scythe has cut more deeply in one spot than another in the garden of flowers. In this case we shall have no blossoms this year and nobody will be happy. There will not be any more seeds sown. Why is it that in some cases only the flower has been cut off, while in others almost the entire plant has been stricken down?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is obvious what the position is. Under special conditions a reduction has had to be made in the vote this year.

I should like to know the conditions. If the members of the committee will take a glance down this column they will find some very interesting facts. First of all, as mentioned by the hon. member for Red Deer, the appropriation for the Canadian Social Hygiene Council is entirely cut off; this appropriation to the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene is reduced by more than fifty per cent, but apparently we conceive it to be necessary to maintain almost the entire expense in connection with the grant to the Chief Constables' Association of Canada and the grant to the Interparliamentary Union, the latter being reduced by only $60. I disagree with the principle enunciated by the Minister of Railways; but if, as he asserts, it is the policy under which these estimates have been cut, surely an explanation should be forthcoming from him why in this case fifty per cent is cut off this appropriation and only ten j>er cent cut off that to the Chief Constables' Association.

While the minister is considering his answer, might I suggest that this is a 'peculiarly inappropriate vote to be cut at this time. A few days ago, in common I assume with a few of the other members of the house, while perusing the columns of a newspaper published in this city, I noticed some rather unfavourable comments in respect of, shall I say the sanity of members of parliament, including members of the government and leaders of the house. If we are to take that editorial seriously, might I suggest that an increase rather than a decrease in this vote might be necessitated? But apart from that and speaking perhaps more seriously, the time in which we live and the nervous strain under which we are all working-I mean the people throughout the country'-would certainly necessitate extreme care and possibly increased expenditure in respect of this particular appropriation. I think it was a mistake, at least in this instance, that the doctrine enunciated by the Minister of Railways in regard to a ten per cent cut, was not adhered to, instead of a fifty per cent cut being made.

The hon. member for Red Deer has not fully explained whether the restoration of the grant to its old standard was in his opinion for the purpose of taking care of the mental condition of members of the House of Commons, or that of the Ottawa Journal.

Supply-Justice

While the minister is cogitating his answer may I say that if one cared to be facetious he might suggest that the economic conditions obtaining in this country under the present government are such that we may need a very large grant to take care of all the people who will become mentally deranged. Speaking seriously, I believe that the economic conditions in this country at the present time are going to increase, and have already increased, the strain upon institutions and people who are caring for the mentally deranged, and I think that this is one of the last votes that should be reduced if the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene is making any proper use of the grant. I say that in all seriousness, and I am surprised that the Minister of National Health would reduce this grant by fifty-five or sixty per cent. Certainly he should explain to the committee why this grant has been reduced from $20,000 to $9,000 at a time like this. We need something more than the simple statement that all these grants are ' being reduced by ten per cent, because the reduction here is over fifty per cent.
This committee is entitled to an explanation, and I for one will not allow the vote to pass until we get one. That is the least we can expect from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have no further
explanation to give beyond the one I have already given.

What is
that explanation?

driving [DOT] some people almost out of their minds; in fact, some men in this country have been driven insane because, of it. How the financial stringency can be given as an excuse for reducing thi-s grant by over fifty per cent is beyond my imagination.

I want to ask a question which may properly come under 'this vote. There are occasions when private citizens, having or thinking they have a claim against the crown, wish to proceed against some body representing the crown, and I understand that before they can do so a fiat must be granted by the Department of Justice permitting them to bring suit. The question arose through a request made to me by one of our returned men. He had got into some dispute with the pension commission and he was under the impression-I am not familiar with all the details-that he was being wrongfully refused payment of pension after thei act had been complied with to the extent of the pension itself being granted in part. He was then advised that the nest step 'to be taken was to proceed against the pension commission, and that in order to do that he had to secure a fiat from the Department of Justice permitting him to bring suit. I am not familiar with the procedure, and I should be glad if the minister would tell me first whether, under any circumstances, suit of tha't nature may be brought ; if so, is it necessary first to secure a fiat? Also, what procedure must be followed in order to make application for that fiat? If the minister can answer that it will enable me to reply to the inquiries made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All actions or suits against the crown
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

can be commenced only by a fiat permitting action to be brought. I do not know the facts of the case to which my hon. friend has referred, but he may take it as the law generally that no suit can be entertained against the crown without the consent of the crown, which is the fiat. Application for a fiat is made to the Minister of Justice, and when granted suit can be brought in the exchequer court. In any reasonable case a fiat is never withheld.
Thank you. If that is the case a person wishing to apply for a fiat simply communicates with the Minister of Justice stating his case and making his request?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a form of petition submitted when a request is made for a fiat. A petition is filed, and then on the recommendation of the minister His Excellency the Governor General endorses it, "Let right be done." That is the fiat.
A copy of the petition may be secured from the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The form of petition is in accordance with the rules of the exchequer court, which are available to anybody.

I should like to refer to the case of Fontaine and Lacasse, who, on account of a miscarriage of justice a few years ago, were sent to a penitentiary. Afterwards it was found that they were innocent. I understand they have made application to the Department of Justice for compensation. To bring the facts clearly before the committee I shall read an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of March 17, 1932:
The Citizen has received a letter from Lionel Fontaine in which he appeals to us again to draw his case to the attention of parliament. This we do in the belief that until some restitution is made a blot will remain on Canada's reputation for impartial justice.
Fontaine is one of the two men (Lacasse is the other) who were charged, "identified," and sentenced as the guilty persons in the robbery of an Ottawa milk salesman in Rockcliffe in the
[Mr. Guthrie.l
fall of 1929. They were given two years and served seven months of that term before their innocence, by an extraordinary turn of events, in which the police had no part, was established.
It is now nearly two years since Fontaine and Lacasse were shown to be the victoms of a miscarriage of justice. But they have received no redress.
Then the closing paragraph is as follows:
Presuming no steps have yet been taken to "amend the incident" it is time that something were done. Fontaine asks on behalf of himself and Lacasse for compensation to the amount he would have earned if gainfully employed during the seven months the two lay in prison innocently convicted. We respectfully call the attention of the authorities to this request once more and suggest that the compensation be paid.	.
I think the request is very reasonable, because had they been falsely accused by a layman he would have had to make compensation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member is no doubt aware of the fact that while we in this parliament make the criminal law of Canada, the Department of Justice or the government does not administer that law throughout the provinces. The unfortunate prosecution which resulted in the conviction of these two young men was undertaken at the instance of the attorney general's department of the province of Ontario. His officers made the arrest and conducted the prosecution; the federal department of Justice had no part in it whatsoever. Conviction was made after a trial in the province of Ontario, and sentence was imposed by a court of that province. The prisoners were ordered to serve their terms in the penitentiary at Kingston. As soon as the true facts were brought to the attention of the former Minister of Justice he recommended that the two young men in question be released. I do not think he had authority to make a payment of money, or to do anything other than he did do-to have the young men released as speedily as possible. This case has been before me at least half a dozen times, and in each instance I have informed the applicants that if they have any redress they must seek it from the legislature of Ontario, in which province the prosecution was instituted. It is one of those unfortunate miscarriages of justice that sometimes take place, but I cannot see that the federal department is in any way responsible for it.

The Minister of Justice has said an injustice was done to these men. Naturally the Canadian people will think they are entitled to compensation. So far as I can learn, no application has been made to the provincial legislature. It would seem that

pressure should be brought upon the provincial authorities by the federal government so that this anomaly may be remedied. From the article appearing in the Citizen one would conclude that these young men think they should receive compensation from federal authorities,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have no reason to think that, because ever since they were liberated they have been informed definitely and on many occasions that any claim to compensation or indemnity they may have should be lodged with the Ontario legislature. They know that; I do not know whether or not they have made application there.
I have learned there is to be some reorganization in connection with the personnel of the penitentiary at Kingston. Is the minister in a position to make a statement in that connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; reorganization is contemplated. We have two penitentiaries at Kingston. One of them is in course of construction, and has hitherto been referred to as the preferred class penitentiary. The name has been changed and it is now known as the Collins Bay penitentiary. That institution was controlled by an acting warden who had never been appointed to the wandenship. Formerly he had been an inspector on the penitentiary staff, and he has now returned to his duties as inspector at Ottawa. Another member of the staff named Allen, who was chief engineer, has been appointed warden of the Collins Bay penitentiary. Warden Ponsford of Kingston penitentiary has retired. The position is now vacant. There is an acting warden in that penitentiary, a man who has been for a long time on the penitentiary staff, but the appointment will be filled by the Civil Service Commission. The advertisement for that position has recently been current, and I think applications are all in and are now under consideration. I do not know what the determination of the commission will be in that respect. There is also another change through the retirement of General Hughes, who for many years was superintendent of penitentiaries. That position is likewise vacant and an advertisement is current by the Civil Service Commission to fill it.

Has the minister any information regarding a criminal by the name of Bagiev? He escaped from Oakalla provincial prison some time ago. It is said he was sentenced to a ten-year term at New Westminster penitentiary and was released after serving only five years. Later he was picked up by the provincial police and put in the
provincial prison at Oakalla. He is now advertised as a very desperate criminal who boasts that he will not be taken alive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I have some information with regard to the case. This man Bagley, or Brown-I think Brown is his correct name-was implicated, with three others, in an armed robbery some six or seven years ago. They were convicted and received fairly long terms in the penitentiary. Brown, or Bagley, was sentenced to a term of ten years and twenty lashes. His three companions in crime were released in 1928 and 1929. Brown was not released at that time. He did receive the lashes that were imposed and has served with remission-because remission is allowed for good conduct-six and a half years of his term. In November, 1930, he was released for deportation to the United States, being an American citizen. He was deported. Subsequently he seems to have again come to Canada in some way or other, and committed a further crime, for which he was placed in the provincial prison at Oakalla, British Columbia. From that prison he escaped, and has since been guilty of some other serious depredation, I do not know exactly of what nature. I believe at the moment his whereabouts are not known, but, I understand, he is regarded as a dangerous criminal.

Is the position of warden at
New Westminster penitentiary being filled?

speechtext:
I must say quite freely
that I have not been consulted about it either directly or indirectly by any member of the commission.

Have any of
them ever been in a penitentiary themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot say as to that,
but I understand that they selected a committee and placed the applications before the committee to deal with. I know of one case -and I fancy that my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition will recall it-where the Civil Service Commission made an appointment some years ago and actually brought the man from Nova Scotia to fill it, but when he got here they reconsidered the matter and told him he could not have the position, and

appointed another man. But I do not know the modus operandi adopted by the Civil Service Commission in regard to these appointments, more than the fact that they advertise the vacancies.

A few years ago a resolution was discussed in this house regarding the advisability of providing work for inmates of penitentiaries with a view to supporting their families. Has anything along that line been considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Nothing along that line
has ever been adopted. I do not think anything of the kind is in force in any prison in the British Empire. I believe in some prisons in the United States something is done in this way, the inmates being paid at the rate of about ten cents a day.

I do not know whether the Prime Minister as yet assumes responsibility for the utterances of the high commissioner or not, but if he does perhaps he will explain ito the committee what the 'high commissioner meant when he said 'the other day, as reported pretty generally in the press of Canada of April 6:
On every hand-
This is referring to the British people.
On every hand it is said that since the reformation there has been nothing of such importance as the economic conference in Ottawa next July.
I have been ait a loss to appreciate the significance of the reference to the reformation in connection with the economic conference, but perhaps the Prime Minister can explain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As far as I know, Mr. Chairman, the remark must have meant that there has 'been an entire reformation of the fiscal system of Great Britain, and 'this is a manifestation of it, being the result of the efforts in that direction.

Then I notice the high commissioner also says:
The conference is spoken of in Great Britain as the new dispensation in British history. Independent of politics, independent of everything else, it is realized that the empire is facing a determination of its independence on international contacts.
Can the Prime Minister explain the sentence, "The conference is spoken of in

Great Britain as the new dispensation in British history"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It marks an epoch probably, and epochs and new dispensations are more or less synonymous. Possibly the high commissioneir thought another landmark in history was -being passed which was very important to the whole British empire. I am bound to say that my attention had not been directed to that particular part of his remarks. The first observation I had seen. Assuming he is correctly reported, I cannot think he meant other than just what is said, that the coming economic conference is a very great and important event in the minds of -many people, that the British public were expressing great hopes and expectations of a favourable outcome of the conference to be held in -this city next July, and that under the newer dispensation of closer trade relations between the various component parts of the empire another -epoch would commence. I imagine the words "new dispensation" were used in that sense, rather than as affording liberty or licence,-if one might use either word-t-o indulge in other than the most hopeful expressions of good will and of belief in the future of the commonwealth of nations under closer union and a new dispensation.

Evidently the high commissioner is indulging in a large measure of prophecy; we hope he may not be humbugging the British public, as well as the Canadian, in what he has had to say. Does that account for the $1,800 additional salary being given to the high commissioner?

As a matter of fact the
salary is lessened by $1,000.

Salaries and expenses of the office of the High Commissioner for Canada, including $1,800 additional salary for the High Commissioner to that authorized by chapter 15, R.S.C.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The increase in this item comes about by reason of the slight change in the standard used for the purpose of determining the amount to be paid by each of the member nations of the league. Our share amounts to not quite thirty-five one-thousandths; the exact figure is 3%9s>i. We pay that proportion of 1,079,669-63 gold francs, or $227,621.10 in gold dollars. The slight change made in the basis of adjustment by the finance department of the League of Nations-for they have a budget, and what amounts to a minister of finance-imposed that amount upon us.

How are the expenses
allocated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The old basis was the
postal union rates. Linder that system rather a heavy burden was imposed upon us, but some adjustments have been made and now we have an arbitrary allotment, fixed by the department of finance of the league. Perhaps the details would take some time to explain, but the representatives of the nations first of all determine how much will be required for the year. This year there is an extra amount in connection with the disarmament conference and the expenses incidental to it. Then thejr apply a principle at which they have arrived, and as a result our share is almost thirty-five one-thousandths. The expenses are divided into 99i parts, of which we pay 35 as our share.

I was wondering if the
question of population had anything to do with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; the question of
population was not regarded as a sound basis upon whioh to determine these contributions when the league was started. I suppose my hon. friend is familiar with the fact that the postal union arrived at certain understandings upon which they classified the different countries, and our original contribution was made under that classification. It imposed upon us rather a heavier burden than would have been the case if population had been the standard, because we occupied a position of somewhat greater importance, from the standpoint of the international postal union, than was indicated by our population. I remember discussing the matter at some length with Sir Herbert Ames when he was attached to the financial section of the league, and he explained to me the difficulties which had been encountered in the early days in arriving at some basis on which the computation could be made. It is not based solely upon population. There were factors which determined the action of the international postal union at one time, and those factors have been considered. Finally the arrangement I have indicated was arrived at, by which the whole cost was divided into 99J shares, our portion being 35.

It always seems
rather strange to me that it is only under an item of expenditure that we have any opportunity of finding out anything definite in connection with our policies with regard to foreign affairs, but apparently this is the only way we can get at it.
There are one or two matters with reference to which I should like the Prime Minister to make some statement. I refer first to Canada's attitude, in the league, with regard to Manchuria and conditions in China. I think almost everyone must have been disappointed at the attitude of the league, especially in the earlier stages of the trouble. I do not know just what is the position at the present moment, but whatever that may be with regard to the league proper, still the league is only a combination of the member nations, and as yet we have not had a statement as to the attitude of Canada as a member of that league. I wish we might have from the Prime Minister some statement with regard to that whole matter.

I do not know whether
the hon. gentleman desires that I should enter into an historical discussion, in the first in-

stance, of the incidents that led up to the present conditions in Manchuria and the difficulties that have been encountered in an amicable adjustment of the differences between Japan and China. If so, I shall have to take another occasion for that, but I should like to remind my hon. friend that Canada was not a member of the council of the league, and of course responsibility for the conduct of the business of the league when the assembly is not in session must rest with the council.
I do not want to interrupt-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is quite all right.

Each member of
the league is at liberty under certain circumstances to make representations to the council with regard to anything that is liable to upset the peace of the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I was only going to point out that the conduct of the league was determined by the council up to the time the assembly'met and that Canada had not membership in the council. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman desires that I should indicate just what steps were taken by the council. I assume that hon. members are all familiar, from reading the newspapers and the official reports that have appeared from time to time, with the steps that were taken by the council. In the end, the assembly was called together, and as it was called together at a time when the representatives of the government were present in Geneva, in connection with the disarmament conference, they were asked to attend the meeting of the assembly. They did attend at that assembly, participated in the discussions, and assisted in arriving at the conclusions which were reached and which, you might say, were practically unanimous as to what position should be taken.
I did not think it would be wise, and I certainly accept the responsibility for having so advised our delegates, that we should endeavour, with the slight knowledge that we possess as compared with those who are constantly in touch with the situation at Geneva, and those who are responsible for the investigations in Manchuria, either to blame or praise this country or the other in connection with matters so serious as those involved in the then differences between Japan and China. But in view of what the hon. gentleman has said, and owing to the fact that I have not brought with me the papers connected with the meeting at Geneva, I shall be glad to let the item stand and indicate to

the committee just what was done so far as we were concerned, the part our delegates took in the assembly, and the opinions which they expressed at that gathering, and which I think would reflect at least the sober, intelligent and moderate judgment of Canadian public opinion. I shall be glad to do that, and the item can stand for that purpose.

Thanks very much. May I ask the Prime Minister, if on some future occasion he brings this matter to the committee, whether he will also be prepared to give the committee some idea as to what instructions have been given to the Canadian delegates to the disarmament conference? That is a matter of general interest to the people of Canada, and it would be well for us to know just where the government stands with regard to the whole disarmament question. Are we prepared to take any sort of lead with regard to such matters? I suppose that at this late hour there is hardly time to go into that, but when the Prime Minister is bringing down other information possibly he will be willing to give some idea as to where our delegates stand at this time.
